```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, fig.align = "center",
  warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, dev = "png", dpi = 150

```

```{r load}
library(censusindia)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## What is included in censusindia?

Census data for every decennial census from 1901 to 2011. Some years also carry
the Primary Census Abstract, which adds households, literacy, Scheduled Caste
and Tribe counts and work status to the population totals. The 2011 abstract
goes down to village and ward.



```{r inventory}
list_census_datasets() |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Population is available across all twelve censuses, 1901 to 2011. 
The detailed abstracts exist for five years only: 1961 (literacy), 1971, 1981, 2001 and
2011. 

## Attach maps

Any indicator can go straight onto the boundaries of its census year:

```{r first-map, fig.height = 7}
get_census(2011, "district") |>
  attach_geometry(2011, geography = "district") |>
  plot_map("population",
    title = "District population, 2011",
    legend_title = "Persons", palette = "blues", trans = "log10"
  )
```

## Census years are not interchangeable

Each year has its own source table, and they carry different columns. 1961 is
a table of literacy rates, state and district only. 1971 and 1981 split by sector. 2011
reaches subdistricts.

```{r geographies}
list_census_geographies() |> count(geography)
```

If you ask for a year and geography that do not exist together, you will get an error
rather than an empty frame:

```{r not-available, error = TRUE}
get_census(1961, "subdistrict")
```

For 1971 and 1981, `sector` defaults to `"total"`. Rural and urban are there too:
```{r sector}
c(
  total = sum(get_census(1981, "state")$population),
  urban = sum(get_census(1981, "state", sector = "urban")$population)
)
```

## Find a variable

All tables share one column schema, and `get_census(variables = ...)` also
computes derived indicators (`literacy_rate`, `sex_ratio`, `sc_percent`,
`st_percent`) where the source counts exist. `list_census_variables()`
lists all 50 variable-geography combinations across 25 distinct variables.

```{r search}
search_census_variables("literacy")

get_census(2011, "state", variables = c("population", "literacy_rate")) |> head(3)
```

Filter states by name or two-letter code:

```{r states}
get_census(1971, "district", state = "MH") |>
  select(district, population) |>
  head(3)

list_states(region = "South")$state_name
```

For 2001 and 2011, `get_census()` reads the Primary Census Abstract
(`census_2001_pca` and `census_2011_pca`), which covers all 593 and 640
districts respectively (unlike `census_population_time_series`, which omits
Sikkim, Mizoram, and Daman & Diu):

```{r pca-vs-timeseries}
c(
  get_census_2001 = nrow(get_census(2001, "district")),
  census_2001_pca = nrow(census_2001_pca),
  get_census_2011 = nrow(get_census(2011, "district")),
  census_2011_pca = nrow(census_2011_pca)
)
```

Literacy, SC/ST and worker counts live in the abstracts, for 2001 and 2011:

```{r pca}
census_2001_pca |>
  summarise(
    districts = n(),
    literate_pct = share(sum(literate), sum(population)),
    worker_pct = share(sum(workers), sum(population))
  )
```

`census_2001_pca_full` is the same 593 districts with the full published
abstract: nineteen indicators, most split by sex, each district given three
times for total, rural and urban.

```{r pca-indicators}
ind <- setdiff(
  names(census_2001_pca_full),
  c(
    "year", "geography", "state_code", "state_name",
    "state_name_harmonized", "district_code", "district", "sector"
  )
)

tibble::tibble(
  indicator = sub("_(male|female)$", "", sub("^(males|females)$", "population", ind)),
  part = dplyr::case_when(
    grepl("(^|_)males?$", ind) ~ "male",
    grepl("(^|_)females?$", ind) ~ "female",
    TRUE ~ "total"
  )
) |>
  group_by(indicator) |>
  summarise(split_by = paste(sort(unique(part)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Which lets you split rural from urban:

```{r pca-demo}
census_2001_pca_full |>
  filter(sector != "total") |>
  group_by(sector) |>
  summarise(
    cultivators = share(sum(main_cultivators), sum(main_workers)),
    agri_labour = share(sum(main_agri_labour), sum(main_workers)),
    hh_industry = share(sum(main_hh_industry), sum(main_workers)),
    other = share(sum(main_other), sum(main_workers)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

1971 and 1981 have their own abstracts in `census_1971` and `census_1981`.
1961 has literacy only. The 1931 caste tables, by province and religion, are in
`census_1931_castes` and `census_1931_exterior_castes`.

## Attach geometry

Districts split and change names between censuses. `attach_geometry()` joins
data to the boundary vintage of its census year:

```{r boundaries, fig.height = 6.5, fig.width = 9}
YEARS <- c(1941, 1951, 1961, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001, 2011)

lapply(YEARS, function(y) {
  get_census_boundaries(y, "state") |>
    sf::st_geometry() |>
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    transform(year = y)
}) |>
  do.call(what = rbind) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 2) +
  theme_census_map(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```


```{r district-vintage, warning = FALSE}
abstract <- census_1971 |>
  at_level("district") |>
  attach_geometry(1971, geography = "district")
series <- census_population_time_series |>
  filter(year == 1971) |>
  at_level("district") |>
  attach_geometry(1971, geography = "district")

c(
  `1971 abstract + 1971` = sum(!sf::st_is_empty(abstract$geometry)),
  `time series 1971 + 1971` = sum(!sf::st_is_empty(series$geometry))
)
```

District maps need the abstract for that year. 

The package parses boundary files once and keeps them for the session.
`clear_geometry_cache()` releases them. `compare_maps()` puts several years on one
color scale. `get_palette()` returns the ramps that `plot_map()` uses.

```{r palette}
get_palette("blue_red")
clear_geometry_cache()
```



## Population Projections

`get_population()` reads the [MoHFW projections](https://nhm.gov.in/New_Updates_2018/Report_Population_Projection_2019.pdf),
which run past the last census. The state table is annual from 2011 to 2036,
with male, female, and total projections across 39 entries (36 states and UTs,
Ladakh, the merged Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu row, and India).

```{r projections-shape}
proj <- get_population(geography = "state")

c(
  entries = dplyr::n_distinct(proj$state_name_harmonized),
  years = dplyr::n_distinct(proj$year),
  first = min(proj$year), last = max(proj$year)
)
```


```{r projections-trend, fig.height = 4}
proj |>
  filter(state_name_harmonized == "India") |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(added = population - lag(population)) |>
  filter(!is.na(added)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, added / 1e6)) +
  geom_col(fill = census_colors()[["accent"]], width = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Millions added that year") +
  theme_census()
```

District projections are available on two boundary systems. `census2011` covers
the 640 Census 2011 districts at five-year steps (interpolated for intermediate
years). `lgd` covers 783 Local Government Directory districts annually from 2012
to 2031, area-apportioned from the Census 2011 age projections.

```{r projections-district}
c(
  census2011 = nrow(get_population(2031, "district")),
  lgd = nrow(get_population(2031, "district", boundary = "lgd"))
)
```

## Data below district level

2011 also has the abstract at the village/ward level. The three tables
together are 63 MB, so the package downloads them on first use and keeps them
in a cache (`census_cache_dir()` gives the location):

```{r detail-use}
census_2011_demographics() |>
  at_level("district") |>
  summarise(districts = n(), population = sum(population))
```

Worker classification is available from `census_2011_workers()` and
`census_2011_marginal_detail()` provides the marginal-worker duration split.
Tribal and language information is also available:

```{r communities}
census_2011_tribes |>
  slice_max(population, n = 3) |>
  select(state_name_harmonized, district, tribe_name, population)

census_2011_linguistic_diversity |>
  filter(coverage >= 0.9) |>
  slice_max(effective_languages, n = 3) |>
  select(district, n_languages, effective_languages, coverage)
```

`coverage` is the share of the district population with a named mother tongue
in C-16. It decreases to 0.04 in parts of Nagaland. There, the unscheduled
languages are in unnamed residual categories. Thus, if you do not filter, these
districts are at the top of the list.
